title: INT 2Fh, the DOS multiplex calls
covers: INT 2Fh, the multiplex interrupt: the calls DOSBox-X's multiplex handlers have a case for.

rows.text: INT 2Fh AX=0800h is the installation check of the DRIVER.SYS support.
AL returns the status: 00h not installed and OK to install, 01h not installed and not OK to install, FFh installed.
The call determines whether the internal support code used by DRIVER.SYS is present; DOS 3.2 and later always have it.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x0800.
The case stores no status in AL, which keeps the 0x00 that selected it; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:313.
The case does not report whether the support code is present: it logs a debug line saying the call is unhandled.
INT 2Fh AX=0801h adds a new block device to the DRIVER.SYS support.
DS:DI points to a drive data table.
On return AX, BX, SI and ES are destroyed.
It moves down the internal list of drive data tables, adjusting the flags word of tables on the same physical drive, and appends the new table to the chain.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x0801.
The case never reads DS:DI; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:313.
The case stores no register, so AX, BX, SI and ES keep their values; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:313.
The case adds no drive data table: it logs a debug line saying the call is unhandled.
INT 2Fh AX=0802h executes a device driver request.
ES:BX points to the device driver request header.
On return the request header is updated as the requested operation says.
The original flags word of the INT call is left on the stack, by the driver's RETF, at least in DOS 5.0 to 6.22.
DOS 3.2 executes this function for any AL from 02h through F7h; DOS 4.0 and later for AL=02h and AL=04h through F7h.
This call is one of several ways in which a device driver request may be invoked.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x0802.
The case reads no request header at ES:BX: its only use of BX is the debug log line at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:313.
The case updates no request header: it stores nothing and only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:313.
The case stores no flags word; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:313.
The case is selected by AX=0x0802 and runs no driver request: it logs a debug line saying the call is unhandled.
INT 2Fh AX=0803h gets the list of drive data tables of the DRIVER.SYS support, in DOS 4.0 and later.
On return DS:DI points to the first drive data table in the list.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x0803.
DS:DI is loaded from the DOS_DriveDataListHead pointer, which the code's own comment calls a pointer to a dummy table.
INT 2Fh AX=1000h is the installation check of SHARE.
AL returns the status: 00h not installed and OK to install, 01h not installed and not OK to install, FFh installed.
If DOS 4.01 loaded SHARE automatically, file sharing stays inactive (undocumented /NC flag) until this call is made.
DOS 5 and later chain to the previous handler if AL is not 00h on entry.
In DOS 3.x any AL other than 00h puts SHARE into an infinite loop.
In PC-DOS 4.00 any AL other than those described puts SHARE into the same loop.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1000.
AL becomes 0xFF only when SHARE is enabled; otherwise it stays 0x00, and 0x01 is never returned.
The case activates no file sharing: it sets AL when SHARE is enabled and returns.
The case tests no AL on entry beyond the AX=0x1000 match and calls no previous handler.
The case contains no loop: it sets AL when SHARE is enabled and returns.
The case contains no loop: it sets AL when SHARE is enabled and returns.
INT 2Fh AH=13h sets the disk interrupt handler, in DOS 3.2 and later.
DS:DX points to the interrupt handler the disk driver calls on read and write.
ES:BX holds the address to restore INT 13 to on system halt or warm boot (INT 19).
DS:DX returns as set by the previous invocation of this function.
ES:BX returns as set by the previous invocation of this function.
IO.SYS hooks INT 13 and inserts one or more filters ahead of the original INT 13 handler.
Before the first call ES:BX points at the original BIOS INT 13, and DS:DX does too unless IO.SYS installed a special hard disk read filter.
Most DOS 3.2 and later disk access goes through the vector in DS:DX, though a few functions still use an INT 13 instruction.
The call is a dangerous security loophole for virus-monitoring software that does not trap it.
Novell DOS 7 IBMBIO.COM before 1995-05-08 trashed AX on return, crashing VGACOPY; later Novell DOS 7 releases preserved AX.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1300.
The case never reads DS:DX.
The case never reads ES:BX.
The case stores no DS:DX.
The case stores no ES:BX.
The case records and hooks no INT 13 vector.
AX is set to 0x0000 on return, where later Novell DOS 7 releases preserve it; the case returns true.

searched.gave: Not applicable: DOSBox-X has no MAME header, and its case 0x1302 carries no comment citing a document.
Nothing found: no Microsoft document read describes INT 2Fh AX=1302h; web search found only the AH=13h entry without AL.
Nothing found: search turned up DOS references and Undocumented DOS PDFs, none read as naming AX=1302h.
Not searched beyond the web search; no page naming INT 2Fh AX=1302h turned up.
Ralf Brown's list has INT 2F AH=13h without AL; its AX=1302h hit is a QEMM QPI table, another interface.

rows.text: INT 2Fh AX=1302h is answered by the same case as AX=1300h.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1302.
AX is set to 0x0000 and the case returns true, with no other register stored.
INT 2Fh AX=1216h, a DOS 3.0 and later internal call, gets the address of a system file table entry.
BX holds the system file table entry number.
On success CF is clear.
On success ES:DI points to the system file table entry.
On success BX holds the relative entry number in the system file table that contains the entry.
On success AX is destroyed.
CF is set if BX is greater than FILES=.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1216.
BX indexes the emulator's own Files[] handle table: its comment says the entry number should coincide with the file handle.
CF is cleared for any BX up to DOS_FILES, including a BX of 16 and above, where the case skips its table walk, and a closed handle.
CF is set when BX is above DOS_FILES, or when the chain of table pieces ends before the entry.
ES:DI is set to the entry for BX below 16 whose file is open, from the walk of the table pieces.
The walk subtracts each table piece's size from a local copy of BX, rel_entry, and uses the remainder as the entry's index within its piece.
AX is set to 0xC000 right after ES:DI is set, for BX below 16 with an open file.
It writes the file's reference count into the first byte of the entry, or zero for a closed handle.
For a handle at or above DOS_FILES it writes open mode 0x02 and zero for attribute, device header, time, date, size and position, plus the file's own device info word.
Otherwise it writes the file's open mode, attribute, time, date, size and position, a device info word from the drive, and the drive's DPB pointer.
It also writes the file name into the entry in FCB style, space padded to 8 and 3 characters.
INT 2Fh AX=1600h is the installation check of Windows enhanced mode.
AL returns the status: 00h means neither Windows 3.x enhanced mode nor Windows/386 2.x runs, and 01h means Windows/386 2.x runs.
For any other AL, AL is the Windows major version number, 3 or higher, and AH the minor version number.
INT 2F/AH=16h is an API for DOS drivers, TSRs and applications to cooperate with multitasking Windows enhanced mode.
The 80286 DOS extender in Windows standard mode also supports certain calls.
This call was the XMS version 1 installation check, now obsolete: use AX=4300h and AX=4310h instead.
AL is 80h for an installed XMS version 1 driver with neither Windows 3.x enhanced mode nor Windows/386 2.x running (obsolete--see note), and FFh for Windows/386 2.x running.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1600.
The 0x0301 answer is given only when secure mode is off and DOSCLIP or TOCLIP runs or a stack test matches; otherwise AX keeps 0x1600.
When the hack matches, AX is set to 0x0301, which puts 0x01 in AL and 0x03 in AH.
AL is never 80h or FFh: the case either leaves AX as passed or sets AX to 0x0301.
INT 2Fh AX=1605h is the Windows enhanced mode and 286 DOSX initialization broadcast.
On entry ES:BX, DS:SI and CX are all zero.
DX holds flags: bit 0 clear for enhanced-mode initialization, set for the Microsoft 286 DOS extender; bits 1 to 15 are reserved.
DI holds the version number, major in the upper byte and minor in the lower.
CX returns 0000h if okay for Windows to load, FFFFh with the other registers unchanged for Windows 3.0 in standard mode, nonzero if Windows should not load.
ES:BX returns pointing to a startup info structure.
DS:SI returns pointing to a virtual86 mode enable/disable callback, or 0000h:0000h.
A driver or TSR may watch the broadcast and answer; one returning CX not zero must show an error message, though Windows95 is reported to load regardless.
Each handler must first chain to the prior INT 2F handler with registers unchanged before processing the call.
A handler needing per-VM data stores the returned ES:BX in the next field of a startup info structure and returns a pointer to it in ES:BX.
A single TSR may set the V86 callback; if DS:SI is already nonzero, the TSR must fail the initialization by setting CX nonzero.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1605.
ES, BX, DS, SI and CX are tested for zero; if any is nonzero a warning about the call chain is logged.
DX bit 0 picks the log text, 286 DOS extender or Enhanced mode, and with DOS/V decides whether the startup info is rewritten.
DI is printed in a debug log line as a major.minor version.
The case ends with return false, passing the call on to the other INT 2F handlers.
With DOS/V and DX bit 0 clear, the caller's BX and ES are saved in the startup segment and ES:BX is set to its start.
When EMS provides one, DS:SI is set to the VCPI vm86 control entry point; when it does not, this block stores nothing in DS:SI.
If enable_a20_on_windows_init is set, the broadcast enables the A20 gate and logs it.
INT 2Fh AX=1606h is the Windows enhanced mode and 286 DOSX exit broadcast.
DX holds flags: bit 0 clear for enhanced-mode exit, set for the Microsoft 286 DOS extender; bits 1 to 15 are reserved.
If the init broadcast fails with CX not zero, this broadcast is issued immediately.
This call is issued in real mode.
The list gives this call no return registers, AX included.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1606.
DX is printed in a debug log line, and bit 0 picks the text, 286 DOS extender or Enhanced mode; the case then returns false.
The case issues no broadcast of its own: it logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:569 and returns false.
The case stores no return register: it logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:569 and returns false.
INT 2Fh AX=1607h is the virtual device call out API of MS Windows.
BX holds the virtual device ID.
CX usually holds the callout subfunction.
AX, BX, CX, DX and ES usually hold the results.
It is more of a convention than an API: a standard way for VxDs to talk to DOS device drivers and TSRs.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1607.
BX 0x15 (DOSMGR) is answered by a switch on CX, BX 0x18 (VMPoll) returns true at once, any other ID returns false.
For DOSMGR, BX 0x15, CX selects a subfunction: 0x0000, 0x0001, 0x0003, 0x0004 and 0x0005; any other value returns false.
Except for BX 0x18, a debug line names the virtual device and prints BX and CX.
INT 2Fh AX=160Ah identifies the Windows version and type, in MS Windows 3.1.
AX is 0000h if the call is supported.
BX holds the version, major in BH and minor in BL.
CX holds the mode: 0002h means standard, 0003h means enhanced.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x160a.
AX, BX and CX are set only when long file names are on and a program-name or stack test matches; the case otherwise returns false.
INT 2Fh AX=1611h, an MS-DOS 7 kernel call, gets the shell parameters.
AX is 0000h if the call is supported.
DS:DX points to the primary shell's executable name.
DS:SI points to the primary shell command line, a counted string.
BH is unknown (00h seen) and BL is unknown (00h and 40h seen).
The call returns the program name and command line from the CONFIG.SYS SHELL= statement.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1611.
The name, 4DOS.COM or COMMAND.COM, is copied into the caller's buffer at DS:DX, not returned as a pointer.
The counted string /P /D /K AUTOEXEC is copied into the caller's buffer at DS:SI, not returned as a pointer.
The strings are fixed in the code, not read from a CONFIG.SYS SHELL= statement.
The call is also refused with false while DOSSETUP or KRNL386 is the running program, a hack for Windows 98 SETUP.
From DOS 7 on AX is set to 0x0000; below DOS 7 the case returns false as its first act, before setting AX.
INT 2Fh AX=1612h, an MS-DOS 7 kernel call, is listed with unknown purpose (GET ???).
AX is 0000h if the call is supported.
ES:BX points to DOS 7 kernel data.
VTD.VXD calls it; one returned item points to the WORD where the default CLOCK$ driver counts days since 1 January 1980.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1612.
Thirty-two bytes of a local buffer, starting 0x01 0x00, are copied to the caller's buffer at ES:BX; no pointer is returned.
From DOS 7 on AX is set to 0x0000; below DOS 7 the case returns false as its first act, before setting AX.
INT 2Fh AX=1613h gets the pathname of the Windows95 SYSTEM.DAT registry file, in the MS-DOS 7 kernel.
ES:DI points to the buffer for the full ASCIZ pathname.
CX holds the buffer size in bytes.
AX is 0000h if the call is supported.
The buffer at ES:DI is filled.
CX holds the number of bytes copied into the buffer.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1613.
The case never reads CX, so the buffer size is not checked.
CX is the length of the path without its terminating zero, which the copy does include.
The path starts as C:\WINDOWS\SYSTEM.DAT.
From DOS 7 on AX is set to 0x0000; below DOS 7 the case returns false as its first act, before setting AX.
INT 2Fh AX=1614h sets the pathname of the Windows95 SYSTEM.DAT registry file, in the MS-DOS 7 kernel.
ES:DI points to the ASCIZ pathname.
AX is the status: 0000h if successful, 1614h if not supported, else the maximum pathname length (004Eh for v4.00.950).
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1614.
From DOS 7 on AX is always set to 0x0000 and the path copy is limited to CROSS_LEN+1 bytes; before DOS 7 AX keeps 0x1614.
INT 2Fh AX=1680h releases the current virtual machine time-slice.
AL is 00h if the call is supported.
AL stays 80h, unchanged, if the call is not supported.
Programs can use it in idle loops to enhance performance under multitaskers.
MS Windows 3 and later, DOS 5 and later, DPMI 1.0 and later, and OS/2 2.0 and later for multitasking DOS applications, support it.
It does not block the program; it just gives up the remainder of the time slice.
Windows-specific programs should not use it.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1680.
When the 'dos idle api' setting is off the case stores nothing, so AL stays 0x80, yet it still returns true.
The case is answered in every DOS version: it tests none.
With 'dos idle api' on, it sets the interrupt flag and halts the CPU.
INT 2Fh AX=1689h is the Windows 3.0 and later KERNEL idle call.
BX holds status flags.
The list gives the return as unknown (???).
The Windows KERNEL idle loop calls it; VMM takes it as a sign of idleness, which generates INT 28 and INT 2F AX=1607h BX=0018h callouts.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1689.
The case never reads BX.
The case stores no register: it returns true.
INT 2Fh AX=168Fh DH=01h is the Windows95 close-awareness query close.
DH is 01h.
DL is 00h, reserved.
AX is the status: 0000h close selected but not acknowledged, 0001h close issued and acknowledged, 168Fh close not selected.
It determines whether the user asked for the application to be closed through the system menu's Close option.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x168f.
The case never reads DH.
The case never reads DL.
The case stores nothing and returns true, so AX stays 0x168F, close not selected, whatever DH holds.
The case never determines a close request: it returns true.
INT 2Fh AX=1A00h is the ANSI.SYS installation check, in DOS 4.0 and later.
AL is FFh if ANSI.SYS is installed.
The call is documented for DOS 5 and later, but undocumented for DOS 4.x.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1a00.
On PC-98 the call returns true with no register stored, because PC-98 MS-DOS does not answer it, as the code comment says.
When ANSI.SYS is not installed the call also returns true with no register stored.
INT 2Fh AX=1700h identifies the WinOldAp version, in MS Windows.
AX stays 1700h if this WINOLDAP version does not support the clipboard.
Otherwise AX is not 1700h: AL is the WINOLDAP major version and AH the minor version.
WinOldAp is a Windows extension giving character-mode applications access to DDE, menus and the clipboard.
This installation check does not follow the usual format of returning AL=FFh.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1700.
The call also returns false for DEFRAG, DISKEDIT, NDD, NDIAGS, UNERASE, UNFORMAT, WINCHECK and a stack-tested INSTALL or INSTALLD.
INT 2Fh AX=1701h opens the clipboard, through WINOLDAP.
AX is nonzero on success.
AX is 0000h if the clipboard is already open.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1701.
Without the Windows arm AX becomes 0x0001 whatever the clipboard state; the Windows arm sets 0x0000 when OpenClipboard fails.
With secure mode on or the clipboard DOS API off, the call returns false and does nothing.
INT 2Fh AX=1702h empties the clipboard, through WINOLDAP.
AX is nonzero if the clipboard has been emptied.
AX is 0000h on failure.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1702.
In the portable code AX is set to 0x0000; the lines that can set 1 are in the Windows, SDL2 and macOS arms.
With secure mode on or the clipboard DOS API off, the call returns false and does nothing.
INT 2Fh AX=1703h sets the clipboard data, through WINOLDAP.
DX holds a clipboard format WinOldAp supports.
ES:BX points to the data.
SI:CX holds the size of the data.
AX is nonzero if the data was copied into the Clipboard.
AX is 0000h on failure.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1703.
Only formats 0x01 and 0x07 are acted on.
In UTF-8 mode the data at ES:BX is read, cut at its first zero, CR LF turned into LF, and handed to DOS_ClipboardSetUTF8.
Each arm takes the number of bytes to read from ES:BX from CX, a 16-bit value.
With secure mode on or the clipboard DOS API off, the call returns false and does nothing.
In the SDL2-or-macOS arm, the text is split into lines, CR dropped, converted from the guest code page, then passed to SDL_SetClipboardText (SDL2) or SetClipboard.
INT 2Fh AX=1704h gets the size of the clipboard data, through WINOLDAP.
DX holds a clipboard format WinOldAp supports.
DX:AX is the size of the data in bytes, headers included, or 0000h:0000h if the clipboard holds none in this format.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1704.
Only formats 0x01 and 0x07 are acted on.
With secure mode on or the clipboard DOS API off, the call returns false and does nothing.
Outside UTF-8 mode, in the non-Windows arm, the text comes from the paste buffer with LF turned into CR LF and controls other than TAB, CR and LF dropped.
INT 2Fh AX=1705h gets the clipboard data, through WINOLDAP.
DX holds a clipboard format WinOldAp supports.
ES:BX points to the buffer.
AX is nonzero on success.
AX is 0000h on error, or when the clipboard has no data in this format.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1705.
Only formats 0x01 and 0x07 are acted on.
With secure mode on or the clipboard DOS API off, the call returns false and does nothing.
Outside UTF-8 mode, in the non-Windows arm, the text comes from the paste buffer with LF turned into CR LF and controls other than TAB, CR and LF dropped.
INT 2Fh AX=1708h closes the clipboard, through WINOLDAP.
AX is 0000h on failure and nonzero on success.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x1708.
Without the Windows arm AX is set to 0x0001; only the Windows arm calls CloseClipboard.
With secure mode on or the clipboard DOS API off, the call returns false and does nothing.
INT 2Fh AX=4680h is the installation check of MS Windows v3.0.
AX is 0000h when MS Windows 3.0 runs in real (/R) or standard (/S) mode, or DOS 5 DOSSHELL is active.
AX is nonzero when there is no Windows, a Windows prior to 3.0, or Windows 3 in enhanced mode.
Windows 3.1 provides an installation check that works in all modes (AX=160Ah).
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x4680.
The case stores no 0x0000 in AX: it returns true with the 0x4680 that selected it still in AX, whatever runs.
INT 2Fh AX=4A01h queries the free HMA space, in DOS 5 and later.
BX is the number of bytes available in the HMA.
BX is 0000h if DOS is not using the HMA.
ES:DI points to the start of the available HMA area.
ES:DI is FFFFh:FFFFh if DOS is not using the HMA.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x4a01.
With a DOS version below 5, DOS_HMA_LIMIT returns 0 and the case replies BX=0000h, DI=FFFFh and ES=FFFFh; DOS_HMA_FREE_START also returns 0.
INT 2Fh AX=4A02h allocates HMA space, in DOS 5 and later.
BX is the number of bytes to allocate.
ES:DI points to the start of the allocated HMA block.
ES:DI may instead be FFFFh:FFFFh.
BX is the number of bytes actually allocated.
BX is rounded up to the next paragraph for DOS 5.0 and 6.0.
The call is not valid unless DOS is loaded in the HMA (DOS=HIGH).
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x4a02.
BX is rounded up to the next paragraph when the DOS version is below 7, so for every DOS 5.x and 6.x and not only 5.0 and 6.0.
DOS_HMA_CLAIMED stops DOSBox-X through E_Exit if the HMA is not enabled, if the allocator has no start yet, or if the allocator would pass the limit.
INT 2Fh AX=4A10h with BX=0000h is the SMARTDRV v4.00 and later installation check, which returns the hit ratios.
CX is EBABh (SMARTDRV v4.1 and later; see the notes in the list) and not 0EDCh.
AX is BABEh if SMARTDRV is installed.
DX:BX is the number of cache hits.
DI:SI is the number of cache misses.
CX is the number of dirty cache elements.
BP is the version in BCD (4.10 = 0410h).
The internal name of SMARTDRV is BAMBI, hence the magic BABE.
Although DS and ES are listed as unmodified, some releases of SMARTDRV seem to trash DS.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x4a10.
The case does not test CX: it only prints CX in a debug line at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:938.
The case stores no AX: it keeps the 0x4A10 that selected it; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:938.
The case stores no DX and no BX; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:938.
The case stores no DI and no SI; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:938.
The case stores no CX; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:938.
The case stores no BP; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:938.
The case stores no DS; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:938.
The case prints a debug line saying the SMARTDRV call is unhandled, with AX, BX, CX, DX and BP, and returns true.
INT 2Fh AX=4A11h with BX=0000h is the DBLSPACE.BIN GetVersion installation check.
AX is 0000h (successful).
BX is 444Dh ("DM").
CL is the first drive letter used by DBLSPACE (41h, 'A', is A:).
CH is the number of drive letters used by DBLSPACE.
DX bits 14-0 are the internal DBLSPACE.BIN version number.
DX bit 15 is set if DBLSPACE.BIN has not yet been relocated to its final position in memory (DBLSPACE.SYS /MOVE).
DBLSPACE.BIN is the resident driver for DoubleSpace, the disk-compression software bundled with MS-DOS 6.0 and 6.20.
The complete DBLSPACE.BIN API is still supported by the DRVSPACE.BIN of MS-DOS 6.22.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x4a11.
The case stores no AX: it keeps the 0x4A11 that selected it; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:941.
The case stores no BX; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:941.
The case stores no CL; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:941.
The case stores no CH; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:941.
The case stores no DX, so no version number and no bit 15; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:941.
The case stores no DX, so it stores no bit 15 either; it only logs at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:941.
The case prints a debug line saying the DBLSPACE call is unhandled, with AX, BX, CX, DX and BP, and returns true.
INT 2Fh AX=4A16h opens the Windows 95 boot log.
AX is the status: 0000h successful, FFFFh boot log file already open, otherwise a DOS error code.
BX is destroyed.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x4a16.
The case opens no boot log file: its body is a return of true.
The case stores no status in AX, which keeps the 0x4A16 that selected it.
INT 2Fh AX=4A17h writes a message to the Windows 95 boot log.
CX is the number of bytes to write.
DS:DX points to the message to write.
The message must include CR-LF if it is desired.
AX is the status: 0000h successful, FFFFh boot log file not open, otherwise a DOS error code.
After writing to the file the call runs the code for INT 2Fh AX=4A21h.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x4a17.
The case writes no boot log file: it prints the message as a BOOTLOG line through LOG_MSG.
The case does not read CX: it gives MEM_StrCopy a limit of 255 bytes for the text and logs it.
The case reads guest memory with MEM_StrCopy at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:946 before logging at 947; AX is not stored.
The case reads guest memory with MEM_StrCopy at src/dos/dos_misc.cpp:946 before logging at 947, so it does run code.
INT 2Fh AX=4A18h closes the Windows 95 boot log.
AX is the status: 0000h successful, FFFFh boot log file not open, otherwise the DOS error code from closing the file.
BX is destroyed.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x4a18.
The case closes no boot log file: its body is a return of true.
The case stores no status in AX, which keeps the 0x4A18 that selected it.
INT 2Fh AX=4A33h checks for MS-DOS version 7, in Windows 95.
AX is 0000h for MS-DOS 7.00 and later.
BX, DX, SI and DS may be destroyed (officially).
Undocumented: DS:DX points to the ASCIZ name of the primary shell executable.
Undocumented: DS:SI points to the CONFIG.SYS SHELL= command line, a counted string.
Undocumented: BH is 0000h, marked with question marks as not understood.
Undocumented: BL is 0000h, marked with question marks as not understood.
AX is nonzero (usually 4A33h) for MS-DOS 6 and earlier or another DOS.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0x4a33.
The case stores no DS and no DX.
The case stores no DS and no SI.
The case stores no BH.
The case stores no BL.
With DOS major version 6 or below, AX keeps the 0x4A33 that selected it and the handler returns false, so INT2F_Handler tries the next multiplex handler.
INT 2Fh AX=B800h is the network installation check.
AL is 00h if no network is installed.
AL is nonzero if a network is installed.
BX holds the installed component flags, and bit 3 is the redirector.
BX holds the installed component flags, and bits 6, 2, 7 and 1 are the server, messenger, receiver and LANPUP (LANtastic 4.0) components.
The component flags in BX are to be tested in the order listed.
The multiplex handler reaches it by its case 0xb800.
The case answers only when enable_network_redirector is set; otherwise it returns false at once.
After the stores the case ends in break, so the handler returns false.

INT 2Fh AX=150Eh gets or sets the volume descriptor preference, in CD-ROM v2.00+.
BX is the subfunction: 00h gets the preference, 01h sets it.
For the get subfunction DX is 0000h on entry.
For the get subfunction DX is the preference settings on return.
For the set subfunction DH is the volume descriptor preference: 01h primary, 02h supplementary.
For the set subfunction DL is the supplementary volume descriptor preference: 01h shift-Kanji.

The MSCDEX handler reaches it by its case 0x150E.
BX=0 stores 0x0100 in DX; the BX=1 branch only compares DH with 1 and, if it differs, stores the AX=1 error and sets CF.
The get branch does not read DX: it only stores 0x0100 in DX.
The set subfunction accepts only DH=1 and fails every other value, 02h included, with AX=1 and CF.
The set branch reads DH only, never DL.
INT 2Fh AX=150Fh gets a directory entry of a CD-ROM, in CD-ROM v2.00+.
CL is the drive number (0=A:).
CH bit 0 is the copy flag: clear for a direct copy, set to copy to a structure that removes ISO and High Sierra differences.
ES:BX points to an ASCIZ path name.
SI:DI points to the buffer for the directory entry.
The buffer must be 255 bytes for a direct copy and 285 bytes for the canonical structure.
CF is set on error.
On error AX is the error code.
CF is clear if successful.
On success AX is the disk format: 0 for High Sierra, 1 for ISO 9660.
A direct copy holds the directory entry: length byte, XAR length in blocks, and the data LBN and the file length, each in Intel then Motorola order.
In a High Sierra direct copy the date and time are 6 bytes at 12h, the bit flags are at 18h and byte 19h is reserved.
In an ISO 9660 direct copy the date and time are 7 bytes at 12h, the seventh the GMT offset in 15-minute units, and the bit flags are at 19h.
In both formats the interleave size is at 1Ah, the skip factor at 1Bh, the volume set sequence number at 1Ch and 1Eh, and the file name length at 20h.
The file name starts at 21h, followed by an optional padding byte when its length is odd, and then the system data.
A canonical entry holds the length of the XAR in logical blocks at 00h and the logical block number of the file start (dword) at 01h.
A canonical entry holds the size of the disk in logical blocks (word) at 05h.
A canonical entry holds the file length in bytes (dword) at 07h.
A canonical entry holds 7 bytes of date and time at 0Bh and the bit flags at 12h.
A canonical entry holds the interleave size at 13h, the interleave skip factor at 14h and the volume set sequence number (word) at 15h.
A canonical entry holds the length of the file name at 17h.
A canonical entry holds a 38-byte ASCIZ file name at 18h.
A canonical entry holds the file version number (word) at 3Eh.
A canonical entry holds the number of bytes of system use data at 40h and 220 bytes of system use data at 41h.
The MSCDEX handler reaches it by its case 0x150F.
The canonical structure stores 0x0800 at 05h, the block size, not the number of logical blocks on the disk.
The 0x40-byte write sends bytes 3Eh and 3Fh from an uninitialized buffer, so no file version number is stored there and the field carries whatever the buffer held.
The branch reads and writes guest memory at src/dos/dos_mscdex.cpp:912-925, logging at 909; the structure has no system use length.
The name is read as a length-prefixed string, the byte at ES:BX giving its length and the name starting at the next byte, not as an ASCIZ name.
The 38 bytes at 18h come from readBuf[21] of the directory record, not the name at 33, at most min(name length, 38) of them, with no NUL or fill.
INT 2Fh AX=1510h sends a device driver request, a CD-ROM v2.10 and later call.
CX is the CD-ROM drive letter, 0 for A and 1 for B.
ES:BX points to a CD-ROM device driver request header, described at AX=0802h.
CF is clear if the device driver has been called; the request header at ES:BX tells whether an error occurred and is updated.
CF is set if the device driver has not been called, with AX the error code (000Fh invalid drive, 0001h invalid function) and the header unchanged.
MSCDEX initializes the request header's subunit field from the drive number in CX.
MSCDEX v2.21 through v2.25, at least, return error code AX=0001h if nested calls are attempted.
The MSCDEX handler reaches it by its case 0x1510.
CF is cleared and the status word written; an unknown function is logged as unsupported and reported done, though the drive's first request reports the error.
No nesting is counted: every request for a valid drive is sent, and only an unknown drive sets CF.
CF is set with 0x0F in AX for an unknown drive; the invalid function code 0x01h is never stored, and the header is left unchanged.
The request is dispatched to callbacks that DOSBox-X installs in its own emulated device header.
